methodological_rigor.justification: The study is a prospective, investigator-initiated, non-randomized single-arm trial (NCT02534675) in 210 evaluable patients with heterogeneous advanced cancers; the absence of a concurrent control arm limits causal inference about the matching-score (MS) effect, as explicitly acknowledged in the Discussion ('association does not necessarily indicate causation'). Statistical methods include Kruskal-Wallis with Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment, Fisher's exact tests, Cox and logistic multivariable regression with HRs/ORs and 95% CIs, and weighted linear regression across five MS strata — generally appropriate, but no a priori power calculation is reported, and the MS >50% dichotomization appears post-hoc without clear pre-specification. Multiple subgroup analyses (TP53-mutant, immunotherapy-treated, OncoKB level 1/2, GI vs non-GI) are reported without a global multiplicity correction. Confounding by indication is a central threat since MS is physician-assigned via MTB; the multivariable adjustment helps but cannot replace randomization.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: Design is a single prospective cohort / non-randomized investigator-initiated trial of a treatment-selection framework, placing it at Oxford 2b. Clinical relevance is high: endpoints are patient-centered (OS, PFS, DCR by RECIST v1.1, Grade 3/4 toxicity) in a pan-cancer advanced/metastatic population, and the paper proposes a concrete translational next step (I-PREDICT 2.0 randomized trial stratified by MS). The dosing-titration framework for first-in-human combinations also aligns with FDA Project Optimus priorities, giving it direct regulatory and practice-relevant traction. It is hypothesis-generating rather than practice-changing on its own, which caps the score below 5.

reporting_quality.justification: Because this is a non-randomized prospective cohort/observational analysis of a single-arm trial, STROBE is the most applicable checklist (REMARK is partially relevant for the MS biomarker component). The manuscript provides a flow diagram (Fig 1A), eligibility concepts, MS definition, trial registration (NCT02534675), multivariable adjustment, and a reasonably complete limitations section, but much methodological detail is deferred to a Data Supplement not fully visible here, and several STROBE items (handling of missing data, loss to follow-up quantification beyond the flow diagram, sensitivity analyses) are not explicitly addressed. The Data Supplement reportedly contains patient-level data (Table S1) and multiple supplemental tables/figures, which is above average for a clinical trial manuscript; no public data repository or analytical code is mentioned.

novelty_literature.justification: The conceptual core — matching score correlating with outcomes under N-of-1 matched combinations in I-PREDICT — has been reported in two prior publications from the same program (refs 21, 22, Sicklick 2019 and 2021), so this is a meaningful extension rather than a first-in-class concept. The novel contributions are the explicit safety/dosing analysis of 103 previously unstudied FDA-approved drug combinations, demonstration of lower SAE rates with first-in-human regimens via intrapatient dose titration, and the linear MS–outcome relationship across five strata. The paper reasonably positions itself relative to NCI-MATCH, MOSCATO, TAPUR, MyPathway, and WINTHER, though none of those tested customized multidrug combinations with intrapatient dose-finding, which is the genuine methodological novelty.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is well organized with a clear introduction, structured Results subsections mapped to the two hypotheses (safety and matching–outcome), and a comprehensive Discussion that explicitly enumerates limitations and proposes a validation trial. The abstract is quantitatively grounded with concrete numbers (210 patients, 157 regimens, 103 novel combinations, 6.5% vs 15.5% SAE rates, HRs for PFS/OS). Figure captions are detailed and largely stand-alone interpretable (Fig 3 and Fig 6 in particular). Minor issues: some redundancy between Results and Discussion, and the Methods section in the main text is extremely brief, deferring almost everything to the supplement.

key_strengths: Large (n=210) prospective pan-cancer cohort with pre-registered trial (NCT02534675) and clinically meaningful endpoints (OS, PFS, DCR, Grade 3/4 toxicity)
Novel safety finding that 103 previously unstudied FDA-approved drug combinations delivered via intrapatient dose titration had lower Grade 3/4 SAEs than established regimens (6.5% v 15.5%, P=.047)
Consistent independent association of higher matching score with longer PFS (HR 0.44) and OS (HR 0.54) on multivariable Cox analysis, with linear MS–outcome gradient across five strata
Transparent and self-aware limitations section, explicitly reframing findings as hypothesis-generating and proposing a randomized I-PREDICT 2.0 trial
key_concerns: Single-arm, non-randomized design means confounding by indication cannot be excluded for the MS–outcome association; MS is physician-assigned via MTB
No a priori power calculation and MS >50% dichotomization appears post-hoc; multiple subgroup analyses without global multiplicity correction
Core finding (MS correlates with outcome) overlaps substantially with two prior I-PREDICT publications (Sicklick 2019, 2021); incremental over the program's own work
No mention of public data repository or analytical code sharing; reproducibility depends on supplement contents
Pan-cancer heterogeneity precludes tumor-type-specific inference, and generalizability to centers without an expert MTB and comprehensive NGS is uncertain
chief_reviewer.rationale: Methodologically competent and clinically important precision-oncology work with a genuinely novel dosing-safety finding, but the central MS–outcome result is incremental to prior I-PREDICT reports and the single-arm design limits causal claims — a strong Tier 2 fit (Cancer Research / Clinical Cancer Research / JCO Precision Oncology caliber) with minor revisions, rather than Tier 1.
